new.title: Meet Frankfurt's whole story at the Historisches Museum
new.desc: The city museum joins the medieval Saalhof by the river, whose Staufer chapel from around 1200 is the oldest surviving building in the old town, with a new building that opened in 2017. Its galleries trace Frankfurt from imperial coronations to banking towers, and a large model shows the old town as it looked before the bombing of 1944.
new.tip: Start with the old town model to understand what the Römerberg area lost and what was rebuilt, then walk out onto the Mainkai right outside.
new.q: Historisches Museum Frankfurt, Saalhof 1, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: See 5,000 years of sculpture at the Liebieghaus
new.desc: A textile baron, Heinrich von Liebieg, built this turreted villa on the Museumsufer in 1896, and since 1909 it has housed the city's sculpture collection. Egyptian, Greek and Roman pieces sit alongside medieval saints and baroque figures, often in the wood-panelled rooms of the old house.
new.tip: Leave time for the café in the villa garden, one of the calmest spots on the south bank.
new.q: Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Schaumainkai 71, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Explore design in Richard Meier's white museum
new.desc: The Museum Angewandte Kunst occupies a bright white building by Richard Meier from 1985, linked to the neoclassical Villa Metzler next door. Inside are furniture, ceramics, books and graphic design from many centuries and cultures, shown in airy rooms with views of the park.
new.tip: The Metzler park around the museum is free and leafy, a good place for a break between Museumsufer visits.
new.q: Museum Angewandte Kunst, Schaumainkai 17, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Step behind the screen at the Deutsches Filmmuseum
new.desc: Since 1984 this villa on the Schaumainkai has been Germany's film museum, now run by the DFF. The permanent exhibition explains how cinema creates its illusions, from optical toys and early cameras to editing and sound, and the in-house cinema shows classics and retrospectives.
new.tip: Check the cinema programme and pair an afternoon in the exhibition with an evening screening.
new.q: Deutsches Filmmuseum, Schaumainkai 41, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Dial up history at the Museum für Kommunikation
new.desc: Behind a glass entrance on the Museumsufer, this museum tells the story of how people have sent messages, from mail coaches and pneumatic tubes to old telephones and computers. Many exhibits are hands-on, which makes it one of the more playful museums on the riverbank.
new.tip: It works well with children on a rainy day; much of the collection is on the lower floor, so do not stop at the entrance hall.
new.q: Museum für Kommunikation, Schaumainkai 53, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Visit the slice of cake: the MMK
new.desc: Hans Hollein's triangular Museum für Moderne Kunst opened in 1991 on a wedge-shaped plot near the cathedral, and locals soon nicknamed it the Tortenstück, the slice of cake. Its collection of art from the 1960s onwards is shown in changing presentations rather than a fixed hang.
new.tip: Walk round the pointed east end of the building to see why the nickname stuck.
new.q: Museum für Moderne Kunst, Domstraße 10, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Count the bullet holes on the Eschenheimer Turm
new.desc: Finished in 1428, this 47 metre gate tower is the best preserved piece of Frankfurt's medieval city walls. Legend says the poacher Hans Winkelsee won his freedom by shooting nine holes in the shape of a 9 into the weather vane.
new.tip: Look up at the vane on top with sharp eyes or binoculars. The tower is a short walk from the Hauptwache along Große Eschenheimer Straße.
new.q: Eschenheimer Turm, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Find the hanging keystone in the Leonhardskirche
new.desc: On the Mainkai stands one of the oldest churches in the city, begun in 1219 on land given by Emperor Frederick II and still showing its Romanesque portals. Look for the small side chapel whose vault ends in a stone that seems to hang in mid-air. The church reopened in 2019 after years of restoration.
new.tip: It is right on the riverside promenade, so step in on a walk between the Eiserner Steg and the Untermainbrücke.
new.q: Leonhardskirche, Alte Mainzer Gasse, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Slip into the Liebfrauenkirche on its sloping square
new.desc: Just off the busy Zeil, this Gothic church run by Capuchin friars has a richly carved Three Kings portal from the early 15th century. Outside, the sloping Liebfrauenberg square is framed by old houses and a baroque fountain.
new.tip: The quiet inner courtyard is a good escape from the shopping crowds.
new.q: Liebfrauenkirche, Liebfrauenberg, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Spot Hindemith's tower in Sachsenhausen
new.desc: The Kuhhirtenturm is the last surviving tower of Sachsenhausen's medieval walls, a stout block just south of the Alte Brücke. The composer Paul Hindemith lived inside it from 1923 to 1927.
new.tip: Look at it from the middle of the Alte Brücke, then walk round into the cobbled lanes of Alt-Sachsenhausen behind it.
new.q: Kuhhirtenturm, Große Rittergasse, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Walk the ring of statues in the Rothschildpark
new.desc: On the edge of the banking district, the former garden of a Rothschild villa is now a public park. Its centrepiece is Georg Kolbe's Ring der Statuen, a circle of bronze figures that offers a calm counterpoint to the towers rising all around.
new.tip: It is a two-minute walk from the Alte Oper and a good place to sit with a coffee before or after a show.
new.q: Rothschildpark, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Pause at the Großmarkthalle memorial below the ECB
new.desc: Martin Elsaesser's huge wholesale market hall of 1928 now forms the base of the European Central Bank headquarters, opened in 2015. From its cellar more than 10,000 Jews from Frankfurt and the region were deported between 1941 and 1945, and a memorial on the east side marks the ramp and tracks they were made to walk.
new.tip: The memorial is outdoors and open at any time. Afterwards walk into the Hafenpark next door for the best view of the bank tower.
new.q: Erinnerungsstätte an der Frankfurter Großmarkthalle, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Book a tour of the Westend Synagogue
new.desc: Built from 1908 to 1910 with Art Nouveau and ancient Near Eastern motifs, the Westend Synagogue is the largest in Frankfurt. It was damaged but not destroyed in the pogrom of November 1938 and was restored to serve the Jewish community again.
new.tip: Visits are only possible on guided tours arranged in advance, so plan ahead and bring ID.
new.q: Westend Synagoge, Altkönigstraße 22, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Circle the moated Holzhausenschlösschen
new.desc: In a small park in the Nordend stands a baroque water castle, rebuilt in the 1720s for the patrician Holzhausen family and still surrounded by its moat. Today it belongs to a civic foundation that holds concerts and readings inside.
new.tip: The park around it is a favourite neighbourhood picnic spot; the U-Bahn stop Holzhausenstraße is a few steps away.
new.q: Holzhausenschlösschen, Justinianstraße, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Laugh along at the Caricatura Museum
new.desc: Near the cathedral, the Caricatura Museum für Komische Kunst is devoted to comic art, above all the Neue Frankfurter Schule of satirists such as Robert Gernhardt, F. K. Waechter and Chlodwig Poth. Their cartoons and verse helped shape German humour from the 1960s onwards.
new.tip: Changing exhibitions bring in cartoonists from across the German-speaking world, so check what is on before you go.
new.q: Caricatura Museum, Weckmarkt 17, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Meet Shock-headed Peter at the Struwwelpeter Museum
new.desc: The Frankfurt doctor Heinrich Hoffmann wrote and drew Struwwelpeter in 1844 as a Christmas present for his son, and it became one of the most famous children's books in the world. The museum in the new old town covers his life, early editions and the many parodies the book has inspired.
new.tip: It is in the lanes between the Römer and the cathedral, so it fits easily into an old town walk.
new.q: Struwwelpeter Museum, Hinter dem Lämmchen, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Learn Jewish Frankfurt at the Rothschild-Palais
new.desc: The Jewish Museum on the Untermainkai reopened in 2020 in the classicist Rothschild-Palais plus a new light-filled building. It tells the story of Jewish life in Frankfurt from the Middle Ages to today and holds the collection of Anne Frank's family, who came from the city.
new.tip: Ask about a combined ticket with the Museum Judengasse, a short walk east along the river.
new.q: Jüdisches Museum Frankfurt, Bertha-Pappenheim-Platz, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Watch the Hammering Man work outside the Messeturm
new.desc: Jonathan Borofsky's 21 metre steel worker has been swinging his arm in front of the trade fair grounds since 1990. Behind him rises the pencil-shaped Messeturm, which at 257 metres was the tallest building in Europe from 1991 to 1997.
new.tip: The arm rests at night, so come by day; the Festhalle/Messe U-Bahn stop is right there.
new.q: Hammering Man, Friedrich-Ebert-Anlage, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: See the tram bursting out of the ground at Bockenheimer Warte
new.desc: A watchtower of 1434 from the city's outer defences gives this busy Bockenheim junction its name. Next to it, a U-Bahn entrance designed in 1986 looks like an old tram car crashing up through the pavement.
new.tip: Come on a Thursday, when the Bockenheim weekly market sets up here from 8 am to 6 pm.
new.q: Bockenheimer Warte, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Look into the Portikus on the river island
new.desc: The Städelschule's exhibition hall stands on a tiny island in the Main, reached from the middle of the Alte Brücke. Christoph Mäckler's narrow house of 2006 hosts shows of contemporary art, and entry is free.
new.tip: After dark the lit building makes a great photo from the riverbank; exhibitions change several times a year.
new.q: Portikus, Alte Brücke 2, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Step into a 1928 home at the Ernst-May-Haus
new.desc: The Römerstadt estate above the Nidda valley was built from 1927 to 1929 under city planner Ernst May as part of the New Frankfurt programme, with flat roofs, gardens and the first fully electrified homes in Germany. One terraced house at Im Burgfeld 136 has been restored as a museum, complete with the famous Frankfurt Kitchen.
new.tip: The museum house has limited opening hours, so check before you go; the estate itself can be walked at any time from the U-Bahn stop Römerstadt.
new.q: Ernst-May-Haus, Im Burgfeld 136, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Spot the ribbed glass of the Westhafen Tower
new.desc: This round office tower of 2004 at the old western harbour is clad in diamond-shaped panes that remind every local of the ribbed Geripptes glass that apple wine is drunk from. Around it, the former harbour basins have become a quarter of flats and marinas.
new.tip: The best view is from the river path or the Friedensbrücke; then walk on through the Westhafen quarter along the water.
new.q: Westhafen Tower, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Drink house cider in the Lorsbacher Thal garden
new.desc: This tavern in the Große Rittergasse traces its tradition back to 1803 and makes its own house apple wine. Beyond that it stocks hundreds of apple wines and ciders, served with Hessian food in a big garden.
new.tip: Ask for a taste of the house Schoppen next to one of the bottled ciders. On weekdays it opens in the late afternoon, at weekends from noon.
new.q: Lorsbacher Thal, Große Rittergasse 49, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Sit under the squirrels' trees at Zum Eichkatzerl
new.desc: One of the oldest apple wine taverns in Sachsenhausen, first mentioned in 1880 as a simple hedge tavern. The name means little squirrel, after the ones living in its garden trees, and the wood-furnished rooms are hung with paintings by Hans Schneider.
new.tip: The summer garden fills up fast on warm evenings, so phone ahead at busy times. It opens in the late afternoon.
new.q: Zum Eichkatzerl, Dreieichstraße 29, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Order a Kochkäseschnitzel at Atschel
new.desc: Atschel in Wallstraße is a classic Sachsenhausen apple wine tavern where the Ebbelwoi comes in a stoneware Bembel. Besides Handkäs and Grüne Soße, try the Kochkäseschnitzel, a schnitzel topped with Frankfurt's runny cooked cheese.
new.tip: Book ahead; if it is full, the staff can point you to their sister tavern Zum Sachs.
new.q: Atschel, Wallstraße 7, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Look for the fir wreath at the Fichtekränzi
new.desc: Since 1849 this little tavern in Wallstraße has served apple wine, and its name comes from the wreath of fir branches that for centuries told passers-by that apple wine was being poured. Inside you sit at long wooden tables with strangers, as Frankfurt tradition expects.
new.tip: Squeeze in and say hello: sharing a table is normal here. In summer the garden is the place to be.
new.q: Fichtekränzi, Wallstraße 5, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Taste self-pressed apple wine at Zum Rad in Seckbach
new.desc: In the old village centre of Seckbach, Zum Rad has been pouring apple wine since 1806 and still presses all of it in house. Its garden hosts seasonal events such as an autumn pressing festival and a small Christmas market.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk up the Lohrberg nearby. It is closed on Tuesdays and opens at lunchtime only on Sundays and holidays.
new.q: Zum Rad, Leonhardsgasse 2, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Eat Backfisch at the Kanonesteppel
new.desc: On Textorstraße in Sachsenhausen, the Kanonesteppel has been a neighbourhood apple wine tavern since 1906. The kitchen serves Frankfurt standards such as Grüne Soße, Sauerbraten and fried fish from lunchtime on, and the summer garden has room for over a hundred.
new.tip: Bring cash, as cards are not accepted, and note it is closed on Sundays.
new.q: Kanonesteppel, Textorstraße 20, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Share Rippchen under the plane trees at Zur Buchscheer
new.desc: On the southern edge of Sachsenhausen, the Theobald family has run Zur Buchscheer since 1876 and presses its own apple wine. The garden, partly shaded by old plane trees, is a classic spot for Rippchen mit Kraut, cured pork chop with sauerkraut.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays and opens at noon at weekends, which makes it a good lunch stop after a walk in the Stadtwald.
new.q: Zur Buchscheer, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Have lunch at Dauth-Schneider in Alt-Sachsenhausen
new.desc: This family-run tavern on Neuer Wall has been pouring apple wine since 1850 and, unusually, its kitchen serves all day from late morning until midnight. Expect Grüne Soße with potatoes, schnitzel and a Bembel on the table.
new.tip: It is one of the easiest places in the old quarter for an early meal when other taverns have not opened yet.
new.q: Dauth-Schneider, Neuer Wall 5, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Head out to Zum Lahmen Esel in Niederursel
new.desc: First mentioned as an inn in 1807, the Lame Donkey is one of the oldest and largest apple wine taverns in Frankfurt, in a listed building in the village of Niederursel. The garden with its old trees is a summer favourite for Grüne Soße and Frankfurter schnitzel.
new.tip: Take the U-Bahn to Niederursel. It is closed on Mondays except public holidays, and has a break between lunch and dinner.
new.q: Zum Lahmen Esel, Krautgartenweg 1, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Drink apple wine in the old walls of Zur Stalburg
new.desc: In the Nordend, Zur Stalburg has served Frankfurt food and apple wine since 1879 inside the walls of a former moated manor. The Stalburg Theater, a cabaret and comedy stage, shares the same address.
new.tip: Pair a meal with a show at the theatre. The kitchen opens at noon every day.
new.q: Zur Stalburg, Glauburgstraße 80, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Take coffee and cake at Café Laumer
new.desc: A Westend institution since 1919, Café Laumer on Bockenheimer Landstraße combines a traditional coffee house, its own pastry kitchen and a bistro. It is the kind of place where regulars have had the same table for decades.
new.tip: Pick your cake at the counter first, then find a seat. It opens daily from 9 am.
new.q: Café Laumer, Bockenheimer Landstraße 67, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Sip a flat white at Hoppenworth & Ploch
new.desc: Frankfurt's best-known speciality coffee roaster started in 2008 and roasts its own beans, with a roasting team led by a German roasting champion. The Nordend café on Friedberger Landstraße is a neighbourhood favourite for espresso and filter coffee.
new.tip: Buy a bag of seasonal beans to take home; they also run barista and brewing courses.
new.q: Hoppenworth & Ploch, Friedberger Landstraße, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Debate over a beer at Club Voltaire
new.desc: Club Voltaire on Kleine Hochstraße is a political pub and cultural club and a long-standing meeting place for Frankfurt's left. Many evenings bring jazz, improvised theatre, talks or film nights alongside the bar.
new.tip: Look at the programme on the website first; it opens at 6 pm and is closed on Sundays unless there is an event.
new.q: Club Voltaire, Kleine Hochstraße 5, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Have breakfast in the baroque Hauptwache
new.desc: The little baroque guardhouse of 1729 to 1730 that gives the city's central square its name has been a café for over a hundred years. In 1833 it was stormed by revolutionaries in the failed Frankfurter Wachensturm.
new.tip: It opens daily from 9 am. Take a window table to watch the square, then dive into the shops of the Zeil.
new.q: Café Hauptwache, An der Hauptwache, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Have a sundowner on the Yachtklub boat
new.desc: The Yachtklub is a bar on a boat moored on the Sachsenhausen bank near the Alte Brücke, looking straight across the Main to the skyline. It hosts concerts and parties through the warm months.
new.tip: It is open from early May to the end of October; come before sunset to get a deck seat.
new.q: Yachtklub, Deutschherrnufer, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Sit in Goethe's garden at the Gerbermühle
new.desc: This old mill on the Main east of Sachsenhausen was the summer home of the banker Johann Jakob von Willemer, where Goethe stayed in 1815 and fell for Marianne von Willemer, the muse of his West-östlicher Divan. Today it is a hotel and restaurant with a big summer garden on the riverbank.
new.tip: Walk or cycle there along the south bank from the city centre; the skyline view from the garden is the reward.
new.q: Gerbermühle, Gerbermühlstraße 105, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Join the Friday crowd at the Schillermarkt
new.desc: Every Friday, stalls line the pedestrian Schillerstraße near the stock exchange with vegetables, cheese, bread and flowers. From late afternoon it turns into a social event as office workers stop for a glass of wine and a snack.
new.tip: The market runs from 9 am to 6.30 pm; come after 4 pm for the after-work atmosphere.
new.q: Schillerstraße, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Drink wine at the Friedberger Markt on a Friday
new.desc: The Friday market on Friedberger Platz in the Nordend is where much of the neighbourhood meets at the end of the week. After shopping for produce, people stand around the wine and food stalls into the evening.
new.tip: It runs from 10 am to 8 pm and is busiest from about 5 pm, so go earlier for quieter shopping.
new.q: Friedberger Platz, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Shop the Markthalle and market in Höchst
new.desc: In the old town of Höchst, the market hall and the stalls on the square outside are the centre of local life on Tuesday, Friday and Saturday mornings. You will find bakers, butchers, cheese and vegetables from the region.
new.tip: It runs from 7 am to 1 pm, so come early and then wander down to the river.
new.q: Markthalle Höchst, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Vote for the best Grüne Soße at the festival
new.desc: Every spring a festival tent on the Roßmarkt celebrates Frankfurt's green sauce, made from seven herbs grown in Oberrad. In the evening shows, guests blind-taste seven versions from local restaurants and vote for a winner, while a free daytime market sells the sauce and its herbs.
new.tip: Evening tickets sell out early; the daytime market needs no ticket.
new.q: Roßmarkt, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Picnic in the Grüneburgpark
new.desc: Frankfurt's largest park inside the inner ring was once a Rothschild estate, laid out as an English landscape park by Heinrich Siesmayer. Today its 29 hectares hold wide lawns, a Korean garden given by South Korea in 2005 and a café in an octagonal pavilion.
new.tip: On sunny weekends the lawns fill with students from the nearby university campus; the Korean garden is the quiet corner.
new.q: Grüneburgpark, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Spend a lazy afternoon in Günthersburgpark
new.desc: This Nordend park was a Rothschild summer estate until Mayer Carl von Rothschild left it to the city, which opened it as a people's park in 1892. It has old trees, open meadows, a big water playground and a copper bull sculpture from 1910.
new.tip: Families love the water play area in summer; pick up picnic supplies on Berger Straße on the way.
new.q: Günthersburgpark, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Visit Grzimek's zoo in the Ostend
new.desc: Founded in 1858, Frankfurt Zoo is one of the oldest in Germany and became world-famous under its director Bernhard Grzimek. Highlights include the nocturnal animal house named after him and the Exotarium with its aquariums and reptiles.
new.tip: The indoor houses make it a decent rainy-day option. The U-Bahn stop Zoo is right by the entrance.
new.q: Zoo Frankfurt, Bernhard-Grzimek-Allee 1, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Swim in the giant Brentanobad
new.desc: Set in old parkland beside the Nidda in Rödelheim, the Brentanobad has a single basin about 220 metres long, often called the largest of its kind in Germany. Big lawns, old trees, beach volleyball and an open-air cinema complete the picture.
new.tip: The water is unheated, so the season runs roughly from May to August depending on the weather. Come on a weekday morning for space to swim.
new.q: Brentanobad, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Skate or shoot hoops in the Hafenpark
new.desc: Opened in 2015 on wasteland left over from building the European Central Bank, the Hafenpark is a busy outdoor sports park on the north bank of the Main. It has a large skate park, a pump track, ball courts and lawns.
new.tip: Even if you do not skate, the edge of the skate park is a great spot to watch, with the ECB tower as backdrop.
new.q: Hafenpark, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Catch a performance at the Mousonturm
new.desc: In the 1920s tower of the old Mouson soap and perfume factory, the Künstlerhaus Mousonturm has been one of Germany's leading houses for contemporary dance, theatre and performance since 1988. The programme also includes concerts and festivals.
new.tip: Tickets are often cheaper than at the big stages, and the foyer bar is lively before and after shows.
new.q: Künstlerhaus Mousonturm, Waldschmidtstraße 4, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Sing along with Eintracht in the Stadtwald
new.desc: Eintracht Frankfurt, winners of the Europa League in 2022, play at the Waldstadion in the middle of the city forest, currently called Deutsche Bank Park. A home game with the whole stadium singing is one of the loudest experiences in town.
new.tip: Tickets go fast, so look at the club's official resale platform. Take the S-Bahn to Stadion and follow the crowd through the trees.
new.q: Deutsche Bank Park, Mörfelder Landstraße 362, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Ride the carousels at the Dippemess
new.desc: Frankfurt's oldest folk festival goes back to a medieval market where potters sold their Dippe, the local word for pots. Today it is a funfair with rides, food stalls and a beer tent on the Festplatz by the Eissporthalle, held for about three weeks around Easter and again for a week in September.
new.tip: Take the U7 to Eissporthalle. The autumn edition is smaller and more relaxed, good with children.
new.q: Festplatz am Ratsweg, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Celebrate Wäldchestag in the city forest
new.desc: On the Tuesday after Whitsun, Frankfurt heads to the Stadtwald around the Oberforsthaus for the Wäldchestag, a forest fair with roots in medieval spring festivities. It was once jokingly called the city's national holiday, because shops closed for the afternoon.
new.tip: Rides and stalls already open over the Whitsun weekend, so you can also go on the quieter days before the Tuesday itself.
new.q: Oberforsthaus, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Watch the Fischerstechen at the Mainfest
new.desc: The Mainfest is a summer fair on the city-centre riverbank that traces its roots to a fishermen's thanksgiving in 1340. Over four days there are rides, stalls and the Fischerstechen, in which two men on boats try to knock each other into the water with lances, and it closes with fireworks.
new.tip: It runs from a Friday to a Monday; the bridges are the best spots for the closing fireworks.
new.q: Mainkai, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Spend an evening at the Oper Frankfurt
new.desc: The Oper Frankfurt on Willy-Brandt-Platz has repeatedly been named Opera House of the Year by the critics of the magazine Opernwelt. It shares its long glass foyer with the city's theatre.
new.tip: Look out for reduced tickets for students and young people, and arrive early to see the golden cloud sculpture hanging in the foyer.
new.q: Oper Frankfurt, Willy-Brandt-Platz, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: See a varieté show at the Tigerpalast
new.desc: Tucked away near the Konstablerwache, the Tigerpalast has been Frankfurt's varieté theatre since 1988. International acrobats, jugglers and comedians perform on a small stage close to the tables, and there is a fine-dining restaurant in the house.
new.tip: Book a dinner and show package for a special night out; shows run in seasons, so check the dates.
new.q: Tigerpalast, Heiligkreuzgasse 16, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Hear a band at the Batschkapp
new.desc: The Batschkapp opened in 1976 as a legendary alternative club in Eschersheim and moved to a larger hall on Gwinnerstraße in Seckbach in 2013. Touring rock, indie and hip-hop acts play here most weeks.
new.tip: The U-Bahn stop Gwinnerstraße is right outside; check the programme for the dates you are in town.
new.q: Batschkapp, Gwinnerstraße 5, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Cycle through the Niddapark
new.desc: The Volkspark Niddatal, created for the 1989 Federal Garden Show, is one of Frankfurt's largest parks, with open meadows, woods and a long stretch of the Nidda river between Ginnheim and Hausen. Its cycle and walking paths are part of the city's GrünGürtel green belt.
new.tip: Follow the river path north to the Römerstadt estate, or south to the Brentanobad for a swim in summer.
new.q: Volkspark Niddatal, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Walk the Berger Rücken to the Berger Warte
new.desc: On the ridge above Bergen-Enkheim, the highest part of Frankfurt, stands the Berger Warte, a medieval watchtower of the city's outer defences. Paths along the ridge give wide views over the skyline, the Main valley and the Taunus.
new.tip: Combine it with a stroll through the old centre of Bergen; late afternoon brings the best light on the towers.
new.q: Berger Warte, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Walk round the Jacobiweiher in the Stadtwald
new.desc: Frankfurt's largest pond was created in 1931 and 1932 in the city forest and named after the forester who planned it. A path circles the shore and crosses the water on a wooden bridge, past sculptures by the cartoonist F. K. Waechter, and herons, cormorants and basking turtles are regular sights.
new.tip: Take tram 17 to Oberschweinstiege and walk a few minutes into the woods; in hard winters people skate on the ice.
new.q: Jacobiweiher, Frankfurt am Main

new.title: Skate laps at the Eissporthalle
new.desc: Opened in 1981, the Eissporthalle on the Ratsweg is home to the Löwen Frankfurt ice hockey team and offers public skating with skate hire. Around the hall runs a 400 metre outdoor ice ring.
new.tip: Combine a public session with a Löwen home game for a full winter day out; check session times, as games and events take priority.
new.q: Eissporthalle Frankfurt, Ratsweg, Frankfurt am Main
